approachQuestion.prompt: Return the greatest product of a nonempty contiguous interval in a signed integer array. Return only the product. Examples: [2,-3,-4] → 24; [-2,0,-1] → 0; [-3] → -3. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 100000; −10 ≤ values[i] ≤ 10. Every product of a contiguous interval fits in a signed 64-bit integer. The input is read-only.

options.text: Initialize high, low, and answer from the first value. At each next x, compute both new extremes from x, oldHigh*x, and oldLow*x, preserving both old extremes until both new ones are ready. Update the global answer from the new high.
options.feedback: A negative multiplier reverses order: the smallest previous ending product can become the largest. Restarting at x and retaining both extremes covers every nonempty ending interval, including zeros.

options.text: Store both minimum and maximum ending products at every index, using the same transition, and return the largest maximum.
options.feedback: This computes the correct result on the whole domain, but retains old states that future transitions never read. Removing those states preserves correctness and reduces auxiliary storage.

options.text: Keep only the maximum ending product, replacing it by max(x,oldMaximum*x).
options.feedback: For [-2,3,-4], this discards the ending minimum -6, so misses the optimal full product 24.

options.text: Initialize the global answer to 1 and otherwise use both extremes.
options.feedback: For [-3], no nonempty interval has product 1; the correct answer is -3.

feedback.reason: Preserve both extremal states when a signed transition can reverse their order.
details: Scan n values once, retaining old minimum and maximum ending products and a global maximum. Compute both new extremes in temporaries before replacing the old ones.

A negative value can turn the smallest ending product into the largest. Preserve both old extremes before computing both new ones; updating one early corrupts the other's transition. A zero naturally restarts candidates.

Update the global answer from the new high.”: A negative multiplier reverses order: the smallest previous ending product can become the largest. Restarting at x and retaining both extremes covers every nonempty ending interval, including zeros.

Removing those states preserves correctness and reduces auxiliary storage.
“Keep only the maximum ending product, replacing it by max(x,oldMaximum*x).”: For [-2,3,-4], this discards the ending minimum -6, so misses the optimal full product 24.
“Initialize the global answer to 1 and otherwise use both extremes.”: For [-3], no nonempty interval has product 1; the correct answer is -3.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Scan n values once, retaining old minimum and maximum ending products and a global maximum. Compute both new extremes in temporaries before replacing the old ones. Analyze this fixed implementation. N=n. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.
Include initialization; treat the stated dimensions as variable parameters within their bounds. Use a word per stored counter or flag, not a packed bitset.

feedback.reason: A fixed number of old/new product scalars handles every input value.
details: Each value requires a fixed number of word multiplications and comparisons. A fixed number of old and new products are live, with no arrays or recursive calls.
“O(N²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The extrema summarize all previous ending intervals, avoiding enumeration of their start indices.
“O(N) time, O(N) auxiliary space”: Only the previous extrema and a global maximum are retained, not an entry per index.
“O(log(N+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Every input value is scanned; keeping extrema does not permit skipping unknown values.
